The key accelerant to Monday's ripping rebound was a shocker. But the level that halted the rally was right where you'd expect.

The S&P 500's 4.7% surge on Monday lifted it out of a steep-sided hole following last week's washout selling storm. Its high for the day was just under 7300, a level last seen on Thursday, corresponding to the index's summertime low and representing the floor of the former multi-month trading range. In other words, the pop stopped at the point from which the tape had broken down; the index slipped three-quarters of a percent from there by the close.

More than a third of the S&P's gain was provided by the 31% jump in Nvidia shares alone following Jensen Huang's stunning reinstatement as Nvidia CEO. Here, too, the stock closed right near the Iran-selloff low, which it cracked through some 12 days ago. It remains under all the relevant moving averages and trend lines.

This isn't to minimize or denigrate these moves of rare magnitude, but simply to place them in context. The market was going to attempt a solid bounce no matter the news. S&P 500 futures were indicated higher by more than 2% even before the Huang bombshell struck before Monday's open.

By near-universal agreement, last week's flush had generated the kind of indiscriminate liquidation, oversold conditions and urgent hedging that typically set up at least a snapback rip. Some of these readings were as extreme as near the April 2025 low following the tariff panic, though not all.

The reinstallation of Huang at the apparent behest of the White House triggered an emotional, spring-loaded ramp in the AI trade, a collective panic by the under-invested. When the government jolts the market with a policy shift like this, it not only assuages a prevailing fear in the market, but it grants psychic permission to investors who were frantically selling one day to ravenously buy back the same stocks the next.

It's slightly ironic, given that a common line last week on the recent market setback was that – unlike in the tariff panic or the Iran war corrections – there was no single policy reversal that could short-circuit the selloff and trigger a ferocious recovery.

And maybe there still isn't. Such one-day comebacks from a deeply oversold state are to be respected but not fully trusted. Looking back at prior one-day gains of such amplitude – or prior sequences of a daily drop and gain of more than 5% in the Nasdaq-100 – generate a fair number of episodes inside of nasty bear markets, along with a few consequential market bottoms.

A few further observations and questions at a potentially tenuous tactical moment for the markets:

-The standard playbook is to assume that we've put in "a low, not the final low." Oversold rallies can carry on a while – say, to the 20-day moving average, which for the S&P 500 is up another 3% from here – without getting escape velocity. Graybeards argue for keeping the market on a short leash, expecting there will at least be a retest sequence. Prudent to assume so, though it's inescapable that V-shaped bottoms have become a bit more common in recent years, as recently as at the end of March, on the merest hint that President Trump would consider ceasing Iran hostilities without forcing open the Strait of Hormuz.

The explosion ripped through one of the city's central squares

A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.

The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.

No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details. Armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by De la Espriella.

Writing on social media, the president said that his government would "bluntly and forcefully" respond, external to "every drop of Colombian blood spilled".

"There will be no impunity and no retreat," he added.

It is the latest in a series of attacks targeting official buildings and security forces' headquarters

Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province.

And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of Cúcuta.

Pope Francis claimed he saw the devil three times over the course of his life, as well as the "gates of hell", according to new extracts from his private diary.

In The Private Diary of Pope Francis, published on Tuesday, a 2021 entry lists the late pontiff as having three visions of the devil: once from a car, another "in the choir loft" during Mass, and a third during a meeting with Vatican officials.

"I can't forget the powerful raspiness of his voice," Francis wrote, recalling one of the visions.

In the diary, written from 1992 to 2024, he also expresses regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, when he was criticised for defending a bishop who was accused of covering up sexual abuse committed by a priest.

Francis, who led the Catholic Church for 12 years until his death in 2025, later apologised and summoned the country's bishops to Rome, where they all offered to resign.

"Devastated because of the situation in Chile," Francis wrote in a 2021 entry.

"It was hard for me to admit what happened in Chile; I didn't think it was so serious."

Of his encounters, which Francis interpreted as meetings with the devil, he said he could not forget the devil's "menacing" eyes.

"He looked at me with flaming eyes... more intense than the previous one. They were like flashes of fire," he wrote of his second vision that he said happened inside a Carmelite chapel while he was archbishop of Buenos Aires.

He said the devil's presence intruded on his journeys, including during the visit to Chile amid the clerical sexual abuse scandal, and a meeting a few days after he had returned to Rome.

U.S. Treasury yields were broadly flat on Tuesday as investors took stock of a speech by John Williams of the New York Fed and looked ahead to a 5-year bond auction due later in the session.

The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, student loans and credit card debt — was flat at 4.911%

The 2-year Treasury note yield, the most sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, also held steady at 4.662% The 30-year Treasury yield — which often reacts the most to geopolitical developments — was unchanged at 5.288%

One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.

Monetary policy will need to adjust to "get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis," Williams, president and chief executive of the New York Fed, said on Monday.

"There is still work to do to get that done," Williams added in comments at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York.

He said the latest economic data shows "the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high."

William's comments come ahead of the December FOMC meeting on 8-9 December. Investors are now pricing in a 100% chance of another interest rate hike, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, with a 25 basis point increase expected.

Later on Tuesday, investors will be watching a $70 billion 5-year Treasury auction as the latest supply test, as well as the consumer confidence print for November. The October reading of the personal consumption expenditures price index, which measures underlying inflation, is due Wednesday. The acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash.

It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff, when its blockbuster drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire.

If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023.

Insmed shares rose 14.2% to $170 in early premarket trading, while Sanofi stock rose 6% in Paris.

Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside.

Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop towards the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete.

While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity.

"Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday.

"Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success," CEO Garijo said in a statement.

"I've never been more confident about Arm's future ... I'm wholly committed to realizing Arm's full potential for many years to come," Haas said in a statement on Monday.

Haas will also assume the role of vice chairman of SoftBank Group, effective December 1, Arm said. Arm is majority-owned by SoftBank. Haas is a board member at the Japanese conglomerate and, in April, took over the reins of SoftBank's international business.

Privacy-focused messaging application Signal is tightening protections against artificial intelligence agents that can access information displayed on users' screens, citing concerns over privacy and security.

Signal said AI agents built into mobile operating systems, such as Google's Gemini and Apple's Siri with onscreen awareness, can "scan" information on users' screens, potentially capturing and storing Signal data outside its control.

The company said it will block screenshots in its iOS app and, on Android, enable screen security when it detects an AI assistant attempting to read the screen.

"We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal — and application developers beyond — lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," Meredith Whittaker, president of the app's nonprofit parent Signal Foundation, said in a Friday blog post.

Signal last year introduced similar restrictions against Microsoft's Recall AI on Windows 11. Its latest move adds to a broader push by companies including United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab to limit or block AI agents over security and for customer-protection concerns.

Whittaker said the new protections do not address every way an agent might gain access to data, including by retrieving content already stored on a user's device.

Signal also warned that third-party agents such as Meta's Muse could gain access to private app content through permissions granted during setup.

"Application-level protections will always have gaps, so the data an agent can reach has to be classified, permissioned and recoverable before the agent arrives," said Tianyi Jiang, CEO of data management and protection software company AvePoint.

AvePoint's State of AI 2026 report found that 88.4% of surveyed organizations had experienced at least one AI-agent-related security breach in the previous year. The survey covered 750 IT leaders globally.

"We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data," said Whittaker.

France's economy is flashing fresh recession warnings as businesses delay decisions ahead of the 2027 election — but resilient industries, progress on the budget and lower energy costs could help keep growth positive.

Business activity declined to a six-month low in November, with manufacturing performing worse than the services sector, according to the S&P Global Purchasing Managers' Index published on Monday.

The French private sector is at its most pessimistic about the coming year since late 2012, excluding the months at the start of the pandemic, according to the survey, with job losses recorded for a seventh straight month.

Among the biggest challenges cited by companies were economic conditions, uncertainty, competition and cost pressures, while frail domestic demand is weighing on sales.

France is heading toward a closely watched presidential election in April 2027, with polling suggesting voters may favor candidates offering a break from the policies associated with incumbent President Emmanuel Macron.

Politico polling this year has consistently indicated the front-runner is far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, who has recently made efforts to appease financial market jitters over France's fiscal sustainability, but has failed to convince many analysts that she can stabilize the country's debt trajectory.

The latest PMI figures add to a run of economic woes for France this year, including a dramatic rise in government borrowing costs, a surprise outlook downgrade by ratings agency Fitch, and a tumbling stock market which has underperformed its European peers.

This has compounded a sense of crisis after hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in October and November to protest underfunding in education, the cost of living and the state of public services and housing.

The latest PMI survey has meanwhile raised the odds of France entering a technical recession — two consecutive prints of negative GDP growth — in the fourth quarter, according to Joe Hayes, senior principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The next print will follow a 0.1% contraction in the third quarter, though a revised Q3 reading is due on Friday.

"The eurozone's second-largest economy is struggling with weak domestic demand, in part due to hesitancy from clients to commit to projects ahead of a highly uncertain election period next year," Hayes said.

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.

Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.

Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.

The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.

Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.

"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.

Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".

Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO may have eased concerns over the chipmaker's leadership, but it has also brought renewed scrutiny to the company's corporate governance and its reliance on its founder.

Huang's abrupt departure and unexpected reinstatement exposed a deeper vulnerability at the heart of Nvidia, industry experts told CNBC, raising questions about board oversight and succession planning.

"What does it mean if you have a company too big to fail or a CEO too big to fire?" Angela Mancini, head of advisory for global risk insights at Dow Jones, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Tuesday.

Mancini pointed to Huang's unusually large number of direct reports as another sign of how heavily Nvidia depends on its founder.

"What does it mean when someone has 60 direct reports and you literally are in a situation where you feel like you can fire them?" she added.

For Nvidia, Huang's return offers an opportunity to address some of the governance issue brought to light by his departure.

Jeff Herbst, managing partner at GFT Ventures and a former Nvidia executive who spent nearly two decades at the company, said he had written to the board late last week calling for Huang's return.

While initially disappointed by the allegations surrounding Huang, Herbst said he came to view the episode as an opportunity for Nvidia to strengthen its governance, succession planning and overall management.

"While a lot of people saw a crisis here, I saw a potential opportunity," he said.

Herbst said Nvidia's management and oversight functions needed to evolve alongside its transformation from a relatively small technology company into one of the world's largest corporations.

Iranian forces said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest in a string of incidents in the waterway, as the U.S. escalates sanctions aimed at cutting off Tehran's financial lifelines.

In a statement carried by state news agency IRNA, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three "offending" oil tankers "suffered a severe explosion and fire after hitting naval mines" in the Strait of Hormuz.

The Guards said one tanker was near the southern coast and two were in the eastern part of the strait. All three were under extensive U.S. military air cover and escort that failed to prevent the explosions.

"U.S. military cover and escort will not replace compliance with maritime regulations and instructions from the IRGC Navy Traffic Control Center," the statement said.

Iranian forces have repeatedly warned commercial vessels that only the northern shipping lane has been approved by Tehran for safe passage, while attacking or threatening ships that use alternative routes near Oman.

The U.S. added a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, to the Gulf last week, joining two other carriers in the fleet enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The tanker incidents came after the U.S. Treasury on Monday announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key personnel as part of what it called "a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks."

Iran's economy has come under growing pressure as Washington expanded sanctions under its so-called "Operation Economic Outcast" since August, aimed at crippling financial networks behind the country's oil revenue.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in Monday's statement, described Iran's economy as "underwater," saying its shadow banking system was "the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime."

The conflict also appears to have extended to cyberspace, with Washington investigating Iran as a primary suspect behind dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday.

China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.

On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India.

China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.

It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.

Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.

The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.

The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.

Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.

Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.

Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
